newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bleak New Year for Fokker as Koreans drop bid.
newsitem.headline: Bleak New Year for Fokker as Koreans drop bid.

text.p: Bankrupt airplane maker Fokker faced a bleak New Year Tuesday after one of its principal suitors finally abandoned a rescue package.
The Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs confirmed it had received a message from the South Korean government ruling out a takeover bid from a consortium led by Samsung Aerospace.
"We have received a fax in which they made their decision," a spokeswoman for the ministry said. She said there were no further details on the decision.
Fokker was declared bankrupt in March after racking up huge losses but was kept alive on a skeleton staff of 650 by court-appointed receivers in the hope of finding a buyer.
As the Dutch government embarked on a frantic international search, Samsung emerged as the most credible saviour after Dutch, Russian and Canadian firms all rejected a takeover.
Dutch media reported that the Samsung consortium, which also included Daewoo, Hyundai and Korean Air, had decided the problems involved were just too big.

The rejection leaves the field open for Russian plane maker Yakovlev, the only company still thought to be interested in saving Fokker, despite concern in the Netherlands over its ability to finance such a large deal.
Russian aircraft company Tupolev ruled itself out of contention in August.
Yakovlev's chief designer said this month that a Fokker purchase was an integral part of the company's plan to secure a 25 percent to 30 percent share of the Russian plane market by 2000.
Alexander Dondukov estimated the deal could cost between $200 and $270 million and said Yakovlev had asked the Russian government to provide additional financial support.
"If the government does not give us guarantees, we are working out three reserve options of our own to close this deal successfully," he said without elaborating.
On Tuesday, however, there was no news from Yakovlev.

One of the main problems facing a potential rescuer is that one of Fokker's most important suppliers -- Shorts of Belfast, which made wings for Fokker F-70 and F-100 regional jets -- decided in November to close down production.
Unable to carry on in limbo, Shorts, part of Canada's Bombardier Inc., cited the failure to find a suitable partner for Fokker as the reason.
Should the Yakovlev deal fail, Fokker is likely to be broken up and sold off, an ignominious end for a proud firm founded in 1919 by Dutch aviation pioneer Anthony Fokker.
It is one of the oldest surviving names in the aviation world and its F27 Friendship turboprop, launched in 1957, was one the industry's biggest commercial successes.
But in recent years Fokker struggled to achieve financial stability and swapped industry partners several times.
In 1993 Germany's Daimler Benz Aerospace took a 51 percent stake in the company but, despite job cuts and tight cost controls, depressed world aircraft markets sent the company deeper into the red.
In January 1996 Daimler said it could no longer bear Fokker's huge losses and cut off all financial aid, forcing the company into bankruptcy two months later.
